one_sentence_idea: Test whether CLIP's poor patch-level segmentation is caused primarily by a small set of high-norm "register-like" artifact tokens rather than by the global contrastive objective itself.

Claim that in fine-tuned open-vocabulary segmentation, replacing CLIP text embeddings with a frozen random orthogonal matrix of class vectors loses almost nothing, showing "language priors" contribute far less than advertised.
Quantify how much of open-vocabulary segmentation's "novel class" performance is predicted purely by the frequency of the class name (and its synonyms) in the pretraining caption corpus.

Show that in "segmenting" multimodal LLMs, localization quality of hidden states monotonically degrades through LLM layers, so the best mask queries come from the earliest fusion layers, contradicting the "deep reasoning improves grounding" narrative.
Test whether the gains attributed to language guidance in VLM-based dense predictors are mostly reproduced by simply running the vision encoder at the higher resolution these pipelines quietly adopt.
Establish that different semantic categories peak at different encoder depths in VLMs, so single-layer feature extraction is fundamentally suboptimal and per-class layer routing is a free lunch.

Show that elaborate prompt templates ("a photo of a {} in a scene") improve open-vocabulary segmentation only by shifting per-class logit priors, and a 1-parameter-per-class bias fitted on a handful of images matches them.
Demonstrate that current referring-segmentation models retain most of their accuracy when the linguistic content of the expression is scrambled, because saliency and object-size priors do the work.

Attribute the chronically blurry boundaries of VLM-based segmenters to spectral aliasing introduced by strided patch embedding, and show an anti-aliased (blur-pooled, overlapping) patch stem fixes boundaries without touching attention.

Hypothesize a non-monotonic relationship where patch-text alignment (dense grounding) peaks at intermediate pretraining scale and then degrades as noisy web captions push the model toward bag-of-words global matching.
Test whether the pretrained weights of the LLM inside reasoning-segmentation systems matter at all, versus an identically-sized randomly initialized transformer trained with the same recipe.

Claim that most of the accuracy loss when running VLM encoders above training resolution stems from naive positional-embedding interpolation, and that a principled 2D spectral resampling closes the gap without any high-res fine-tuning.

Measure how much "novel class" performance of open-vocabulary detectors/segmenters survives when images visually similar to benchmark novel-class instances are deduplicated out of the vision-language pretraining set.

Show that the family of training-free attention modifications (value-value attention, self-self attention, correlation reweighting) used to make CLIP segment is functionally equivalent to simple spatial smoothing of the patch-text similarity map.

Argue that region-level contrastive pretraining objectives for VLMs add little beyond global objectives trained with aggressive multi-crop augmentation, because both induce the same patch-level invariance structure.

Test whether the celebrated ability of multimodal LLMs to output boxes/points reflects genuine internal grounding or merely the formatting distribution of instruction-tuning data, by probing grounding before and after instruction tuning with format-neutral probes.
Quantify a granularity-interference effect where training VLMs with box-level grounding annotations degrades their latent pixel-level (mask) separability relative to models trained with none.

Demonstrate that the now-dominant recipe "SAM proposals + VLM labels" systematically fails amorphous stuff regions, so reported open-vocab mIoU improvements are concentrated entirely in thing classes.

Characterize a negative interference law where adding more candidate class names to an open-vocabulary segmenter's prompt set monotonically degrades per-class IoU of the original classes due to probability mass competition among correlated text embeddings.

Build a dense-prediction cue-conflict benchmark (texture of class A pasted into shape of class B) to show language-supervised segmenters are dramatically more texture-biased than supervised segmenters, inverting the classification-level finding that CLIP is shape-biased.
Show that mIoU of open-vocabulary segmenters drops more from replacing class names with common synonyms than from strong image corruptions, i.e., the text tower is the weakest robustness link.

Claim that at fixed compute, the mIoU variance across feature-upsampling strategies (bilinear, JBU, learned guided filters) exceeds the variance across frozen VLM backbones, inverting the field's attention allocation.
Show that averaging text embeddings over automatically retrieved WordNet synonyms/definitions per class equals gradient-based prompt tuning for open-vocabulary segmentation at zero training cost.

Establish that in multi-source grounding fine-tuning of VLMs, final performance per source is dominated by which data appeared in the last fraction of training, making curriculum claims mostly ordering artifacts.

Show that most of the accuracy collapse when moving open-vocabulary segmenters to remote sensing or medical imagery is recovered by correcting class-prior and scale statistics, without touching the representation.

Contradict the belief that dense prediction needs all tokens by showing segmentation mIoU degrades more gracefully under token merging/pruning than classification accuracy does, because local redundancy is higher than global.

Test whether the intermediate reasoning text in "reason-then-segment" VLMs carries any information used by the mask decoder, by corrupting the rationale while holding the final hidden state pathway intact.

Attribute the emergence of patch-level alignment in contrastive VLMs to the statistics of hard negatives within batches (co-occurring concepts forcing spatial disambiguation), predicting that batch composition manipulation alone can create or destroy dense grounding.

Validate (or refute) the implicit assumption that cheap frozen-feature segmentation probes rank backbones the same way full fine-tuning does, which underlies nearly all "foundation model dense benchmark" papers.

Explain why queries like "everything except the road" or "the cup that is not red" fail in text-driven segmenters: negation requires set-complement operations that cosine-similarity scoring cannot represent, and quantify the failure with a constructed negation benchmark.

Measure attention flow to show that after the first few LLM layers, hundreds of visual tokens are effectively ignored and their information is routed through a handful of "carrier" tokens, implying most visual KV-cache is dead weight.

Test the belief that the "modality gap" (separated image/text cones in CLIP space) hurts downstream performance, by showing gap size is controlled by temperature initialization and its removal changes nothing on transfer tasks.
Show that the MLP-vs-QFormer-vs-cross-attention projector debate in VLM assembly is confounded by output token count, and at matched visual token budget all projectors perform equivalently.

Characterize which capabilities die first as visual tokens are compressed: a capability-resolved bottleneck curve showing VQA saturates at very few tokens while counting, OCR, and spatial relations degrade at predictable, distinct compression thresholds.
Quantify how much of multimodal benchmark performance survives random spatial shuffling of visual patch embeddings, exposing which "understanding" results require no spatial structure at all.

Test whether the gains from unfreezing vision encoders during VLM training are reproduced by tuning only LayerNorm/bias parameters, implying the encoder learns no genuinely new features during multimodal alignment.

Systematize "language-prior-corrected" scoring where each VLM's benchmark score is reported as improvement over its own image-blind version, revealing that model rankings change substantially under prior correction.

Challenge the claim that interleaved image-text pretraining creates few-shot multimodal ability, by testing whether single-image-trained models given enough visual context tokens at inference perform comparable in-context learning.

Show that compositional failures of LLaVA-class models (attribute binding, word order) are inherited from the vision encoder's contrastively-trained feature geometry, not from the LLM, by swapping encoders with different composition sensitivity.

Establish compute-matched trade-off curves showing that for fine-grained perception benchmarks, spending FLOPs on higher input resolution beats spending them on LLM parameters by a wide margin, contradicting default scaling allocation.

Test a LIMA-style hypothesis for VLMs: a few hundred carefully formatted visual instruction examples achieve most of what 600K-sample instruction datasets achieve, since tuning teaches response format rather than visual capability.

Localize object hallucination in VLMs to a small set of attention heads where language-prior signals override visual evidence, and show that inference-time down-weighting of those heads reduces hallucination without retraining or decoding tricks.

Attribute VLM failures at multi-image tasks (attribute swapping across images, wrong-image references) to inadequate encoding of image boundaries in the token stream, and show cheap boundary tokens/2-level positions fix most of it.

Provide a task taxonomy showing early-fusion and late-fusion VLMs are equivalent at matched compute on recognition and knowledge tasks, with early fusion winning only where iterative visual re-attention is required (counting, spatial relations, fine OCR).

Show that VLMs develop sink behavior on the first visual token(s), absorbing attention that would otherwise reach detail-bearing tokens, and that sink-aware attention renormalization improves fine-grained tasks for free.

Demonstrate that vision encoders' zero-shot ImageNet accuracy — the default selection criterion — poorly predicts their quality as VLM towers, and captioning-pretrained encoders outperform contrastive ones for assembly despite worse zero-shot numbers.

Test whether the raster-scan serialization of visual patches — an arbitrary choice — measurably biases VLM spatial reasoning (e.g., better horizontal than vertical relations) and whether Hilbert-curve or column-major orders shift the bias predictably.

Decompose the improvements of multi-crop "AnyRes" schemes to show much of the gain comes from feature averaging across overlapping crops (a denoising ensemble) rather than from genuinely finer spatial sampling.

Show that agentic look-again pipelines (model crops a region, re-encodes, answers) provide gains that a fixed heuristic — zoom to the most attended region — matches, deflating the "visual reasoning" framing to a resolution patch.

Claim the visual-token distribution mismatch (mean/covariance) with the LLM embedding space explains most of the frozen-vs-finetuned encoder gap, fixable by one whitening-coloring transform fitted without labels.

Document a perception-interference effect where, holding the vision tower and tuning data constant, larger LLM decoders perform worse on purely perceptual tasks because stronger language priors override visual evidence more aggressively.

Test whether few-shot multimodal ICL uses exemplar image-label pairings for task learning or merely for output-space priming, by measuring performance under systematically corrupted exemplar pairings.

Show that VLMs' inability to report where things are (absolute coordinates) stems from projector-induced destruction of positional phase information, fixable by concatenating explicit coordinate channels — no scaling required.

Quantify the fraction of each popular video-LLM benchmark solvable from one uniformly sampled frame plus language priors, producing a "temporal necessity score" that likely exposes most benchmarks as near-frame-solvable.

Test whether the popular practice of concatenating multiple vision encoders (e.g., CLIP+DINOv2) helps because of "complementary semantics" or simply because it ensembles different effective receptive fields and resolutions — reproducible with one encoder at multiple scales.

Propose and validate that the entropy profile of text→vision attention during generation predicts a VLM's fine-grained accuracy better than parameter count or benchmark aggregates, providing a task-free intrinsic diagnostic.

Measure the collateral damage of end-to-end VLM tuning on the vision encoder's transferable representation quality, testing the belief that joint tuning is harmless or beneficial for the tower itself.

Attribute a specific, predictable class of OCR errors in VLMs (digit substitutions, decimal misplacements) to subword tokenization of numerals in the language decoder rather than to visual encoding limits.

For each multimodal benchmark, replace the image with the model's own generated caption and measure the score retained, yielding a "vision necessity" coefficient that likely exposes many benchmarks as caption-sufficient.

Test the "platonic representation" hypothesis concretely by transplanting a projector trained for encoder-A/LLM-B into encoder-C/LLM-B after only a cheap linear stitch, predicting near-full performance if semantic geometries are truly convergent.

Attribute fine-tuning loss spikes to specific, re-identifiable training samples with characteristic gradient geometry (high norm, low alignment with the average gradient), showing spike prediction and prevention via sample screening.
Derive and empirically validate a scaling rule for how optimal LoRA learning rate must change with rank and layer width, replacing the folklore "LoRA needs ~10× higher lr" with a predictive law.

Test the claim that learning-rate warmup in fine-tuning exists solely to let Adam's second-moment estimates stabilize, by replacing warmup with a proper v-initialization from a few estimation-only batches.

Show that most catastrophic forgetting during instruction/multimodal fine-tuning is caused by drift of embedding and unembedding matrices rather than changes in transformer blocks, so freezing those two matrices retains generality at no adaptation cost.
Validate attention-entropy collapse in a pretrained checkpoint as a cheap forward-only predictor of downstream fine-tuning instability, enabling checkpoint screening before any tuning run.
Look for delayed-generalization (grokking) dynamics when fine-tuning VLMs on small structured datasets, where val performance jumps long after train convergence, controlled by weight decay strength.

Systematically quantify run-to-run variance (seed + data order) of standard fine-tuning recipes on popular multimodal benchmarks and compare it against the margins by which recent papers claim improvements.

Show that the rapid feature destruction in the first steps of full fine-tuning is driven by cold-started Adam statistics (huge effective steps), and warm-starting optimizer state removes most of the LoRA-vs-full-FT forgetting gap.

Localize fine-tuning loss spikes to gradient amplification through LayerNorm/RMSNorm scale parameters in low-loss regions, and show that a reduced lr on norm parameters alone eliminates spikes without slowing adaptation.
Isolate low-precision attention-logit accumulation as a cause of divergence when fine-tuning on longer contexts than pretraining, showing fp32 attention (only) restores stability at negligible cost.

Explain why fine-tuning on model-generated (self-distilled) data is empirically smoother than on human data by showing self-generated targets induce lower gradient-norm variance at matched task shift, formalizing why synthetic-data recipes stabilize training.

Refute the mental model that LoRA approximates full fine-tuning in a low-rank subspace, by showing LoRA and full FT converge to functionally different solutions with distinct generalization and forgetting profiles even when full-FT updates are post-hoc rank-reducible.

Test whether the top Hessian eigenvalue (or SAM-style sharpness proxy) of a checkpoint predicts its fine-tuning spike propensity and stable-lr range, giving a principled checkpoint-selection criterion beyond validation loss.

Test whether a weight-space EMA of an unstable fine-tuning run silently tracks a high-quality solution even through loss spikes, implying spikes are excursions around a sound mean trajectory rather than trajectory derailments.

Localize a class of fine-tuning instabilities to rare tokens with large unembedding norms, where a few target tokens produce exploding per-token losses, and show per-token gradient clipping outperforms global clipping.

Establish that unfreezing the vision encoder during VLM training has a phase boundary: unfreezing before the projector converges causes irreversible representation collapse, while after it, unfreezing is uniformly safe — turning two-stage folklore into a measurable criterion.

Test the counterintuitive hypothesis that models pretrained on aggressively filtered, high-quality data are more brittle under fine-tuning (narrower stable-lr range, more forgetting) because their representations are sharper and less redundant.

Reinterpret gradient clipping during fine-tuning as implicit data curation — the steps it truncates correspond to identifiable low-quality or mislabeled samples — and show explicit removal of those samples beats clipping.

Decompose the benefit of layer-wise learning-rate decay (LLRD) in fine-tuning to show it is functionally equivalent to training early layers for fewer effective steps, and that simple early-layer freezing schedules reproduce it.

Explain oscillatory divergence in multimodal preference tuning (DPO/RLHF variants) as a degenerate feedback loop arising when reward model and policy share vision-encoder features, and show de-correlating the towers stabilizes training.

Test whether LoRA's celebrated forgetting advantage over full fine-tuning survives when both methods are matched on total functional change (update norm or KL from base), rather than on epochs and default lrs.

Contradict the norm-tuning intuition (BitFit-style) by showing that *freezing* LayerNorm/RMSNorm scales during fine-tuning removes most instability while leaving final task performance unchanged, because norm scales are high-leverage, low-information parameters.

Test the scale-dependence of the abandoned progressive-unfreezing technique, hypothesizing that it becomes beneficial again at 7B+ parameters where cold full-parameter fine-tuning damages high-leverage layers before optimizer statistics stabilize.

Document a non-monotonic epoch-performance curve in instruction tuning where benchmark scores dip around train-set interpolation and recover with continued training, implying popular 1–3-epoch heuristics stop inside the dip.

Characterize when and why held-out instruction loss stops correlating with benchmark performance during fine-tuning, giving a measurable "decoupling point" after which loss-based decisions (early stopping, lr selection) become actively misleading.

Show that reshuffling the order of an identical fine-tuning data mixture changes final benchmark scores by as much as swapping between competing published mixtures, undermining mixture-attribution claims in data-recipe papers.

Test the landscape-vs-data explanation of recurrent loss spikes by comparing standard rollback-and-skip-data recovery against rollback-plus-parameter-noise, which should work better if spikes stem from entering pathological curvature regions rather than from bad batches.

Show that placing adapters in attention vs. MLP blocks yields identical in-distribution fine-tuning results but systematically different out-of-distribution robustness, because MLP adapters edit stored knowledge while attention adapters edit routing.

Map fine-tuning into two phases divided by a critical learning rate: below it, representations stay near init (adaptation); above it, they reorganize globally (CKA-to-init collapse) — with benchmark consequences that make the boundary, not the lr value, the object to tune.

Test why interleaving text-only batches during multimodal fine-tuning prevents language-capability forgetting: the standard rehearsal-content explanation vs. the hypothesis that any gradient of matched scale on the language pathway (even from random text) rebalances update norms and prevents drift.

Demonstrate that linear-probe accuracy — the field's default representation-quality metric — fails to predict how useful features are to realistic nonlinear heads under distribution shift, and propose a "tunability probe" that does.

Show that the leading PCA directions of self-supervised features encode photometric and camera nuisances (lighting, blur, JPEG), and simply deleting the top-k components improves k-NN and few-shot transfer.
Test the assumed harm of dimensional collapse in contrastive learning by constructing models with controlled effective ranks and showing transfer performance is flat over a wide collapse range.
Catalog invariances that SSL models acquire without corresponding augmentations (viewpoint, occlusion, illumination direction), and identify which dataset symmetries — not objectives — supply them.

Show that whether a model is pretrained with CLS-token or mean-pooled objectives — usually treated as an implementation detail — determines the gradient distribution over patches and thereby the dense-task quality of patch tokens, independent of the objective family.

Explain the puzzle that masked-image-modeling features probe poorly but fine-tune excellently by showing their advantages live in high-frequency, nonlinearly-coded components that linear probes cannot read but fine-tuning can exploit.

Establish that the depth at which representations are most transferable moves systematically toward earlier (relative) layers as models scale, making the last-layer convention progressively wrong and predictable via a scaling law of "representation peak depth."

Quantify what the near-universal practice of L2-normalizing features throws away, testing whether feature norms carry transferable signal (familiarity, image quality, object count) that norm-aware transfer methods can exploit.

Show that after simple feature whitening at transfer time, the performance differences among major SSL methods (contrastive, distillation, redundancy-reduction) largely vanish, implying much of the method literature differs in second-moment structure, not information content.

Attribute the object-centric character of SSL representations to the random-resized-crop policy rather than to dataset content, by training on scene-centric data with crop distributions manipulated to be object-covering vs. scene-covering.

Establish that k-NN retrieval quality and linear-probe accuracy measure distinct representation properties (local metric fidelity vs. global separability), that models trade them off in characteristic family-specific ways, and that downstream tasks split cleanly by which axis they need.

Show that the temperature in contrastive objectives controls the granularity level (instance vs. fine class vs. coarse class) at which features separate, enabling granularity-targeted pretraining with a single scalar.

Test whether the celebrated superiority of modern SSL (DINOv2-style) over supervised pretraining survives when supervised training is given equal data scale via weak labels, modern augmentation, and matched schedules — or whether "SSL is better" is a data-scale confound.

Show that adding register tokens changes the fundamental locality structure of patch representations (patch tokens become more local as registers take over global aggregation), with consequences beyond artifact removal for dense and correspondence tasks.

Exploit the hypothesis that patch features within a single object span a low-dimensional subspace while boundaries mark rank transitions, enabling training-free object discovery from local rank statistics and giving a new geometric definition of "objectness" in ViT features.

Challenge the necessity of exponential-moving-average teachers in self-distillation SSL by testing whether infrequent hard teacher snapshots (copy every k steps) reach the same quality, isolating what property of the teacher trajectory actually matters.

Run a meta-evaluation showing that popular representation-similarity metrics (CKA, SVCCA, Procrustes) fail to predict whether two models' features are functionally interchangeable (via stitching or head transfer), and derive which metric properties are needed for functional prediction.

Test whether the practical differences between supervised, contrastive, and generative pretraining reduce to how much they rely on the image phase spectrum (structure) vs. amplitude spectrum (texture statistics), yielding a single Fourier-based signature that predicts downstream behavior.

Show that rare/tail classes are well represented in frozen-feature geometry (recoverable with few-shot exemplar matching) even when linear probes trained on the full imbalanced distribution fail them, relocating the long-tail problem from representation to readout.

Quantify the effect of near-duplicate density in pretraining data on representation geometry, testing whether dedup-level explains more variance in downstream quality than the choice among modern SSL objectives.

Explain the persistent underperformance of video-pretrained encoders on static image tasks via a specific mechanism — temporal-invariance objectives collapse pose/state distinctions that static recognition needs — and validate by controlling the invariance horizon.

Demonstrate that mid-network features are systematically more robust to distribution shift than the penultimate features everyone uses, so the standard practice of building on final-layer features actively sacrifices robustness.

Test how much head training actually contributes on top of modern frozen backbones by comparing trained MLP heads against frozen random-feature heads (random MLP + linear readout), predicting near-parity that exposes "head engineering" as low-value on strong features.

Systematically test whether vision (and vision-language) embedding spaces support word2vec-style linear analogies over visual attributes (red car − red + blue ≈ blue car), mapping which attribute families are linearly factored and which are entangled.

Show that the running/adaptive normalization statistics of a network encode enough dataset identity to classify which domain a model was tuned on — and exploit this as a fast domain-shift detector and transfer-compatibility test.

Probe whether CLIP-style embeddings encode approximate object counts as a monotone direction (emergent numerosity), challenging the belief that counting requires explicit supervision or architectural machinery.

Validate a data-centric predictor of SSL quality: the estimated mutual information (or proxy overlap statistics) between augmented positive pairs on a corpus predicts final transfer accuracy across augmentation policies, enabling policy selection without full training runs.

Overturn the universal discard-the-projector convention by showing projector features are superior for fine-grained and instance-level transfer, because the projector holds the invariances while the backbone retains nuisance detail — the standard story backwards for a class of tasks.

Test whether per-class representation quality follows the same log-linear dependence on pretraining exposure frequency across supervised, contrastive, and self-supervised paradigms — refuting the belief that SSL is inherently fairer to rare classes.

Show that a model's position on the shape-texture bias spectrum is continuously controllable via the crop-scale distribution during pretraining, collapsing the shape-bias literature's paradigm comparisons into a single augmentation parameter.

Replace the folklore that "middle timesteps give the best diffusion features for segmentation" with a characterization showing the optimal timestep varies systematically by semantic granularity (parts vs. objects vs. scenes), making timestep a controllable granularity selector.

Test whether the celebrated zero-shot localization of text-to-image cross-attention maps is attributable to the frozen text encoder's representations rather than to anything learned by generative training, using matched text encoders in discriminative pipelines.

Run the missing controlled comparison — generative (diffusion) vs. discriminative (contrastive) pretraining at strictly matched data, compute, and architecture — to isolate what generative pretraining actually adds for dense prediction.

Quantify how texture hallucination in modern perceptual SR systematically corrupts downstream segmentation/recognition (inventing plausible-but-wrong material and class evidence), and propose semantic-consistency as a mandatory SR evaluation axis.

Test whether image restoration (denoising) removes informative signal — sensor noise correlates with materials, depth, and lighting — such that segmentation on restored images is worse than on raw noisy images for models trained appropriately.

Show that reported gains from adding diffusion-generated training images to segmentation datasets are mostly reproduced by reweighting/oversampling the real data to the same class-frequency profile the synthetic data induces.

Use human-indistinguishable diffusion-generated images as a diagnostic set: any accuracy drop of a recognition/segmentation model on them (relative to real images of the same content) measures the model's reliance on natural-image statistical shortcuts invisible to humans.

Use inversion-based object insertion/removal to build counterfactual scene pairs and measure, causally, how much modern segmenters rely on context vs. local evidence per class — replacing correlational context studies.

Characterize systematically when text-to-image attention maps used to auto-generate image-mask training pairs produce corrupted supervision ("attention leakage" onto associated regions like shadows and reflections), yielding quantitative laws of where free synthetic mask data can be trusted.

Extract amodal (occlusion-completed) segmentation from off-the-shelf inpainting diffusion models — by inpainting the occluder and reading the revealed object extent — testing whether generative models implicitly learned object completion that discriminative amodal methods must supervise.

Empirically test a proposed correspondence: features learned by denoising at noise level σ match (in transfer behavior and CKA) features learned contrastively with augmentation strength calibrated to the same information removal, unifying generative and discriminative SSL on one axis.

Show that dense-prediction studies using Stable-Diffusion features inherit a hard resolution/fidelity ceiling from the 8×-downsampling VAE, and that conclusions about "diffusion features" drawn from latent-space models substantially understate pixel-space diffusion capabilities.

Establish an inverse relationship between SR perceptual quality (human preference) and machine-task fidelity (detection/segmentation accuracy on SR outputs), showing the field's optimization target actively harms the growing machine-consumer use case.

Test whether the reported adversarial/OOD robustness of diffusion-based zero-shot classifiers reflects the generative paradigm or simply their orders-of-magnitude larger test-time compute, by giving discriminative models matched inference-compute via ensembling and test-time augmentation.

Characterize self-consuming training loops (models trained on model-generated images) for dense tasks, hypothesizing that spatial/boundary fidelity degrades generations earlier than class-frequency statistics, so segmentation canaries detect collapse before classification metrics move.

Use the disagreement among independent blind restoration models (or one model under seed resampling) as a zero-training uncertainty map for downstream segmentation — regions where restoration is ambiguous are exactly where semantic predictions should not be trusted.

Test whether personalization techniques (textual inversion / DreamBooth) that learn a concept token from ~5 images provide, via cross-attention readout, a few-shot segmentation mechanism competitive with purpose-built few-shot discriminative methods.

Test whether diffusion-harmonized copy-paste augmentation (removing lighting/boundary inconsistencies) produces segmenters that score *lower* on the training-distribution benchmark but generalize better across datasets, because vanilla copy-paste teaches an exploitable paste-artifact cue.

Validate text-to-image generation frequency (how often unprompted attributes appear) as a calibrated instrument for auditing the training corpus's conditional biases, turning generators into measurement devices for dataset bias that annotation audits cannot scale to.

Track the emergence of segmentation-usable structure across diffusion pretraining checkpoints, testing whether dense semantic knowledge appears early (with generation quality irrelevant) — implying cheap, short-trained diffusion models suffice as dense feature extractors.

Make the contrarian case that GAN discriminator/generator features carry sharper boundary information than diffusion features at matched scale, because adversarial objectives concentrate model capacity on exactly the high-frequency structure that likelihood-weighted diffusion training downweights.

Test whether unconditional diffusion models yield dense features nearly as good as text-conditioned ones, challenging the assumption that language conditioning is what organizes diffusion representations semantically.

Extract and quantify implicit 3D/depth knowledge in image diffusion models by analyzing how denoising trajectories treat geometry (e.g., disocclusion behavior, perspective-consistent completion), testing whether generative pretraining learns usable depth without any 3D labels.

Challenge the restore-then-analyze deployment pattern by showing that training segmenters directly on realistically degraded (compressed, low-light) images beats pipelines that restore inputs at test time, across matched degradation severities.

Test whether reported gains from super-resolving inputs for small-object detection vanish when the detector is simply trained and run at the matched effective resolution, exposing SR as an expensive resampling operator in this role.

Use inpainting to replace object interiors with context-consistent but object-inconsistent content, measuring per-class how much segmentation decisions are driven by surrounding context rather than object appearance — a clean instrument for the context-shortcut question.

Test the hypothesis that generative (diffusion) features excel at part-level correspondence while discriminative SSL features excel at instance-level discrimination — a principled division predicting which paradigm serves which dense task.

Develop and validate a falsifiable decision rule: generative augmentation improves a segmentation task if and only if a measurable mode-coverage gap exists between the real training set and the target distribution that the generator demonstrably covers.

Show that heavily stylized (non-photorealistic) generated scenes train segmentation models as well as photorealistic ones at matched layout/annotation diversity, refuting the assumption that closing the realism gap is the key to synthetic data utility.

Test whether video generation models implicitly solve temporal correspondence — readable as object tracking from their spatiotemporal attention — providing supervision-free tracking/video-segmentation and evidence that generation learns object permanence.

Test whether disagreement among LLM/VLM annotators concentrates on the same items where humans disagree — i.e., whether machine disagreement is a valid measurement of intrinsic label ambiguity or a different phenomenon entirely.

Quantify how much repeated sampling of the same VLM ("self-consistency") inflates apparent annotation confidence because same-model errors are strongly correlated, and derive a corrected confidence estimator from cross-model agreement.

Test whether the "hardness" signal used to route annotation cascades (cheap model first, escalate hard items) is a task-general property of images or task-specific, determining whether routing models can be trained once and reused.

Demonstrate that optimizing annotation-guideline prompts for LLM annotators shifts the resulting label distributions in ways that materially change trained-model behavior — making "ground truth" an artifact of prompt engineering choices that are never reported.

Characterize the geometric error structure of VLM/foundation-model-generated segmentation masks (systematic dilation/erosion, corner rounding) and show that models trained on such labels inherit measurable, correctable boundary offsets.

Exploit the generation-verification asymmetry by designing annotation pipelines where LLM agents only verify or choose among candidate labels (produced by cheap specialized models), testing whether verify-only pipelines dominate generate-then-filter at equal compute.

Test the claim that requiring chain-of-thought rationales improves LLM annotation accuracy, hypothesizing instead that rationales leave accuracy unchanged but make erroneous labels much easier to detect post-hoc (by humans or auditor models).

Show that classic active learning breaks under LLM annotation because uncertainty-based acquisition preferentially selects exactly the items where LLM labels are least reliable, creating a feedback loop that concentrates label noise where the student is most sensitive.

Demonstrate that established noisy-label learning methods, built for (conditionally) independent human noise, systematically fail on LLM-annotated data whose errors are confident, correlated, and prior-structured — and characterize the new noise model needed.

Measure the contamination effect when the same foundation model family both annotates a dataset and is fine-tuned on it, testing whether apparent quality gains are partially circular (the student is rewarded for reproducing its own priors, not for learning the task).

Build a systematic taxonomy of VLM annotation errors on objective visual attributes (color, count, material, orientation) and show errors are predictable from language co-occurrence statistics — enabling prior-corrected annotation without any visual improvement.

Establish the precise condition under which debate/discussion between VLM annotators improves label quality — predicted to be error anti-correlation between agents — and show that same-family debate (the common setup) fails this condition and can amplify shared errors.

Quantify how mid-annotation updates of commercial LLM/VLM APIs shift label distributions within a single dataset, and measure the downstream effect of such invisible temporal seams on trained models and benchmark comparisons.

Map the per-task-type accuracy of VLM annotators against crowdworkers to test the hypothesis that their difficulty profiles are inverted — machines better at relations, reading, and consistency; humans better at counting, fine discrimination, and unusual instances — deriving an empirically optimal division of labor.

Treat multiple prompt-variants of VLM annotators as weak labeling functions whose confusion matrices can be estimated and, uniquely, *manipulated via prompt design* — bringing Snorkel-style aggregation theory to machine annotation with a controllable diversity dial.

Test whether decomposing dense annotation into counterfactual queries ("if this region were removed, would the object still be complete?") yields more accurate mask boundaries from VLM annotators than direct "segment the object" instructions.

Quantify the trade-off when detailed VLM-generated captions supervise segmentation vocabularies: hallucinated nouns inject false classes at a measurable rate while true novel nouns extend coverage — determine the operating points where caption supervision is net-positive.

Characterize the convergence of bootstrapped self-annotation (model labels data, retrains on it, repeats) for dense tasks, testing whether the process has a predictable fixed point strictly below the initial annotator's quality and identifying which interventions (confidence gating, disagreement injection) raise it.

Audit deployed machine-annotated datasets for fossilized position/order biases (first-option preference, recency effects in candidate lists) and measure how these structured artifacts propagate into models trained on the data.

Measure the "self-generated easiness" effect: referring expressions, questions, and captions produced by VLMs for benchmark construction are systematically easier for VLMs to solve than human-authored equivalents on the same images, inflating reported progress.

Show that annotating the same images via prompts in different languages produces systematically different label distributions (category boundaries, attribute salience), demonstrating that machine-annotated "ground truth" silently inherits one language's ontology.

Test whether training on full label *distributions* elicited from LLM annotators (via calibrated probability queries) outperforms hard labels with label smoothing, distinguishing whether machine-annotator uncertainty carries real information about item ambiguity.

Demonstrate that imperceptible or innocuous-looking image perturbations can reliably flip VLM annotator outputs, enabling scalable data poisoning through public data that later gets machine-labeled — and measure how such poisoned labels propagate to student models.

Measure diversity decay in the self-referential data flywheel where models generate instruction/annotation data for their successors, testing whether linguistic and task-type diversity contracts generation-over-generation even as quality metrics rise.

Quantify the anchoring effect when human annotators correct LLM pre-labels — measuring how far final "human-verified" labels drift toward machine suggestions relative to blind annotation — and derive the true cost of the speed-accuracy trade in hybrid pipelines.

Deploy VLM agents as error auditors (not annotators) over classic vision benchmarks, and test whether correcting the discovered label errors changes published model rankings — turning the known "benchmarks have errors" observation into a measured ranking-stability result.

Characterize the scaling behavior of agentic annotation quality with decomposition depth — an agent that recursively splits "segment the dog" into part- and boundary-level queries — testing for a predictable quality-vs-cost law and its saturation point.

Test the data-centric claim that having LLMs generate *confusable class descriptions* (hard negative definitions) to guide targeted negative mining improves fine-grained datasets more than adding equivalent budgets of positive examples.

Test for lineage bias in machine-annotated benchmarks: evaluation sets labeled by a model family systematically advantage later models of that family (shared priors, formats, blind spots) over equally capable models from other lineages.

Derive and validate an allocation rule for splitting annotation budgets between humans and LLM annotators based on measured human-machine error *correlation* per task stratum, showing it dominates the standard practice of allocating by error rate and cost alone.

Show that a linear probe on intermediate features predicts a model's own errors substantially better than its softmax confidence, revealing an internal "self-error signal" that standard readouts discard.

Establish that the order in which training examples are forgotten (under continued training on new data) is highly stable across architectures, seeds, and even paradigms — making forgetting order an intrinsic, model-free property of data.

Document a non-monotonic relationship between labeled-data quantity and fine-tuned dense-model quality, where intermediate dataset sizes underperform both smaller and larger ones — sample-wise double descent in a practically relevant regime.

Characterize the puzzling asymmetry whereby sparse trainable subnetworks (lottery tickets) found on one task often transfer to different tasks, yet fail to transfer across random seeds of the same task — inverting the intuitive generalization hierarchy.

Show that the emergence (or absence) of structured Gabor-like and color-opponent filters in a ViT's patch-embedding layer is a reliable early diagnostic of training health, predicting final performance within the first fraction of training.

Demonstrate that classes whose decision boundaries in feature space are geometrically irregular (high curvature, fragmented regions) are precisely the classes that fail under distribution shift — a measurable geometric fingerprint of fragile classes.

Quantify how much of a network's early-layer feature quality arises independently of label content by training with fully random labels and measuring transferability layer by layer, separating "data-driven" from "supervision-driven" representation depth.

Quantify the underappreciated instability whereby segmentation outputs for a fixed image change depending on what other images share its inference batch (through batch normalization or cross-batch statistics), violating the implicit determinism assumption of evaluation and deployment.

Test whether the classic "networks over-rely on high-frequency shortcuts" narrative inverts for modern large-scale-pretrained ViTs, which may be *more* sensitive to low-frequency (global structure) perturbations than to high-frequency noise.

Document a monotonic rise in error correlation across independently developed vision models over the last decade — an emerging monoculture where new models make the same mistakes — and quantify its consequences for ensembling and benchmark headroom.

Show that images seen during pretraining retain anomalously stable features through subsequent fine-tuning (relative to unseen images of the same distribution), creating "memorized anchors" that shape what fine-tuning can and cannot change.

Characterize the surprising robustness of trained ViTs/VLMs to swapping adjacent transformer blocks at inference, mapping where the network is "order-sensitive" and what that reveals about the computational role of depth.

Establish that per-pixel segmentation decisions stabilize at characteristic depths (easy interior pixels early, boundary/rare-class pixels late), and exploit this "pixel prediction depth" phenomenon for adaptive-compute segmentation with per-pixel early exits.

Quantify the "sparse evidence" phenomenon: final-layer decisions of ViTs rest on a remarkably small number of patch tokens regardless of object size, and measure the sufficiency and necessity of those few patches for the decision.

Test whether purely discriminatively trained networks show a likelihood-accuracy coupling — being more accurate on images they can implicitly compress/reconstruct better — revealing a generative substrate inside discriminative learning.

Show that the large fraction of functionally duplicate units in trained networks can be pruned without harm *after* training but cannot be removed *before or during* training without severe damage — establishing redundancy as scaffolding required for optimization, not representation.

Document "capability resurrection": behaviors removed by fine-tuning (e.g., a suppressed classification bias or forgotten task skill) spontaneously reappear after further fine-tuning on unrelated data, revealing that suppression edits are shallow and reversible perturbations.

Test whether human-alignable, monosemantic units in vision models appear at characteristic width thresholds — an interpretability phase transition — implying narrow models are not just weaker but structurally less interpretable per unit.

Characterize the learning-order phenomenon in dense prediction where boundary localization is acquired earlier in training than interior classification — contradicting the coarse-to-fine assumption — and exploit it for principled early stopping and curriculum design.

Test whether a fixed random initialization that performs well on one dataset also performs well on unrelated datasets and tasks — i.e., "lucky inits" are init-intrinsic rather than init-task matches — with implications for init reuse as a free performance lever.

Show via layer-wise readout that vision-model decisions are essentially fixed by mid-depth and that the final third of layers primarily reshapes confidence (calibration and margin structure), redefining what "deep" buys at inference.

Quantify a capture phenomenon in feedforward vision models whereby adding a salient but task-irrelevant object far from the target measurably degrades target recognition/segmentation — despite zero pixel overlap — mapping the "attentional budget" of architectures.

Characterize the set of images misclassified by essentially all models ("universal residue") and test whether membership is predictable from simple image-intrinsic statistics — making the ceiling of benchmark progress a measurable property of data, not models.

Test the contrarian hypothesis that certain training loss spikes are followed by measurable *improvements* in generalization relative to spike-free counterfactual trajectories — spikes as basin-escaping exploration rather than pure pathology.

Show that while aggregate accuracy rises smoothly, individual class accuracies improve via abrupt, step-like transitions at class-specific times — a staircase of per-class phase changes hidden by averaging — and identify what triggers each step.

Investigate the surprising effectiveness of weight-averaging models fine-tuned on *different tasks* (a cross-task soup), testing whether the average outperforms each specialist on its own task's OOD variants — implying task-specific solutions share a common beneficial direction.

Show that learned positional embeddings absorb dataset-specific spatial priors (sky-up, subjects-centered, ground-below) that measurably help ID performance but systematically harm transfer to rotated, aerial, or unconventional-framing domains — PEs as a hidden bias store.

Quantify the anomalous sensitivity of state-of-the-art models to global mean shifts (DC component / brightness) that survive standard normalization — a trivial-seeming perturbation causing outsized accuracy drops that the augmentation pipeline was supposed to have solved.

Document that networks become functionally more linear (lower effective nonlinearity, better low-order approximability) late in long training runs, and show this predicts the empirical observation that late checkpoints distill into small students far better than accuracy-matched early checkpoints.

Show that fine-tuning batch size systematically trades in-distribution accuracy against OOD robustness even when runs are matched on ID validation loss — small batches buy robustness with noise — making batch size a hidden robustness hyperparameter reported by nobody.

Test the assumption that pretraining should always prefer more unique data by comparing multi-epoch training on a curated subset against single-epoch training on the full corpus at exactly matched compute.

Challenge the assumption that input-dependent attention is the essential ingredient of ViTs by training scale-matched models with fixed (learned-but-static) token-mixing matrices and measuring exactly which capabilities require dynamism.

Test the assumption that human annotation defines the quality ceiling by comparing models trained on original human labels vs. model-relabeled versions of the same images, evaluated on independent human-verified gold sets and transfer tasks.

Decompose the celebrated benefit of pretraining on larger-vocabulary datasets (21k classes vs. 1k) to test whether gains derive from label-space richness or simply from more images, by ablating vocabulary at fixed image count.

Refute the folk equivalence "augmentation ≈ more data" by comparing online augmentation against training on a materialized, statically augmented dataset of matched effective size, isolating the stochastic-regularization component of augmentation from its data-quantity component.

Test the assumption that segmentation training requires precise boundary annotation by training with deliberately coarsened masks (blobs, polygons, scribbles) plus boundary-agnostic losses, measuring how much final boundary quality actually derives from label precision versus from image evidence.

Re-examine the accepted practice of testing at higher resolution than training (and its "fix" via resolution fine-tuning), testing whether the benefit is an artifact of object-size distribution matching that disappears under scale-aware evaluation.

Test the persistent belief that class-balanced or class-diverse batches matter for training quality, hypothesizing that at modern batch sizes and schedule lengths, batch composition effects on final models are statistically zero.

Characterize the regime where few-shot fine-tuning of foundation models *underperforms* their own zero-shot behavior — testing the default assumption that any labeled target data should be used for adaptation.

Test the assumption that softmax cross-entropy is a necessary ingredient of large-scale visual classification by training scale-matched models with pure regression losses onto fixed class-anchor embeddings, examining what (if anything) the softmax geometry contributes.

Test whether easy-to-hard curriculum benefits — a persistent community belief — survive when baseline training has properly tuned learning-rate schedules and augmentation ramps, hypothesizing curricula mostly compensate for untuned baselines.

Test the assumption that hyperparameter/checkpoint selection requires validation data from the target distribution, by measuring how often selection on a *different* dataset picks the same winner — potentially eliminating validation-split costs for many workflows.

Challenge the depth-oriented design of dense-prediction backbones by testing whether wider-shallower models dominate deeper-narrower ones at matched compute for segmentation — the opposite of classification-era intuitions the field inherited.

Perform the missing causal audit of the community's continued use of ViT attention maps as explanations, measuring across models and tasks how well attention agrees with causal attribution (deletion/insertion effects) and when the practice actively misleads.

Audit the universal practice of freezing BatchNorm statistics during detection/segmentation fine-tuning — inherited from small-batch-era constraints — testing whether it silently costs accuracy under modern batch sizes and normalization variants.

Test the assumption that test-time augmentation (TTA) is a benign accuracy booster, hypothesizing that TTA gains occur precisely where models are miscalibrated or shortcut-reliant — making TTA gain a diagnostic of model pathology rather than a free lunch.

Re-test the assumption that pretrained initialization always dominates random initialization by mapping the crossover frontier (labels × task type × architecture) where from-scratch training catches up, updated for modern ViTs, recipes, and dense tasks.

Test the foundational assumption that contrastive methods require large negative pools (huge batches or memory banks), hypothesizing that with retuned temperature and schedule, a few dozen negatives match tens of thousands — collapsing a major systems requirement.

Decompose multi-task pretraining benefits by comparing multi-task models against single-task models trained on the *pooled images* (with only one task's labels), testing the assumption that task diversity itself — rather than image diversity — improves representations.

Re-audit label smoothing — a near-universal default — testing the hypothesis that its apparent generalization gains are largely evaluation artifacts (better ECE, minor top-1 noise) while it measurably damages feature transferability, distillation, and rare-class geometry.

Test the belief that ViTs inherently need heavy augmentation (RandAugment, mixup, cutmix) by checking whether longer schedules with tuned optimization at larger data scale eliminate the augmentation requirement — reframing augmentation as an optimization crutch of the ImageNet-1k regime.

Test the assumption that good out-of-distribution detection requires specialized training (outlier exposure, contrastive OOD objectives) by showing simple density estimation on frozen foundation-model features matches or beats trained detectors across standard benchmarks.

Quantify how much spatial position ViTs can recover with position embeddings removed entirely — via content cues like vignetting, chromatic aberration, and layout statistics — testing the assumption that PEs are a necessity rather than a convenience.

Test whether the encoder-decoder-with-skips design (UNet-style), assumed necessary for precise dense prediction, is matched by plain single-stream ViTs with simple learned upsampling once pretraining is strong — relegating skip architecture to a small-model-era artifact.

Test the assumption that ensembling diverse architectures beats ensembling seeds of one architecture, hypothesizing that convergent training data and recipes have erased the architecture-diversity premium in the modern era.

Test the assumption that longer pretraining monotonically improves transfer by measuring downstream fine-tuning quality across pretraining checkpoints, hypothesizing a transfer peak followed by decline (ossification) even as pretraining metrics improve.

Audit whether hard-example mining — folklore from the OHEM/SSD era that persists in pipelines — adds anything on top of modern loss functions (focal, sample-reweighting) and augmentation, hypothesizing full redundancy.

Test the assumption that segmentation improvements from global-context modules (large kernels, global attention, context pooling) come from using long-range information, by measuring effective receptive fields and performing context-ablation at inference — hypothesizing gains are parameter/optimization effects with decisions remaining local.

Test the textbook assumption that weight decay prevents overfitting in large-scale training, against the mechanistic alternative that its role is controlling effective learning rate through weight-norm dynamics — with the regularization story predicting effects that fail to materialize.

Challenge the accepted claim that freezing pretrained backbones (or linear probing) preserves OOD robustness better than fine-tuning, by testing whether the effect is an artifact of measuring robustness on shifts aligned with the pretraining distribution — with the conclusion reversing on shifts aligned with the target task.

Predict a null result for the popular family of attention-guided data augmentation methods (crop/mask where the model attends), hypothesizing they fail to beat random-policy baselines once tuning budgets and augmentation strength are matched.

Test the null hypothesis that pretraining on synthetic formula-generated images (fractals, procedural textures) provides no transfer advantage over training from scratch with modern augmentation at matched total compute.

Predict that architectures discovered by neural architecture search for segmentation/detection do not outperform hand-designed baselines once both are trained with identical modern recipes — the reported gains having come from recipe co-optimization.
Test the null that jointly learning depth and semantic segmentation — a canonical "synergistic" task pair — provides no benefit to either task over single-task models at matched capacity and compute.

Extend the classic attribution sanity checks (parameter randomization, data randomization) to the modern ViT explanation stack (attention rollout, ViT-specific Grad-CAM variants, relevance propagation), predicting widespread failure that the community has not registered.

Test whether claimed emergent capabilities of VLMs at scale (sudden appearance of counting, OCR, spatial reasoning) disappear when measured with continuous proxies instead of thresholded accuracy — predicting smooth capability growth misread as emergence.

Predict a null for the widespread practice of masked-autoencoder self-pretraining on small domain-specific corpora (tens of thousands of medical/aerial images) before fine-tuning, against simply fine-tuning a general checkpoint or training from scratch with strong augmentation.

Test the null that distilling an ensemble into a single student transfers its accuracy but not its OOD robustness or calibration — the properties for which ensembles are actually valued — making "distill the ensemble" a false economy for reliability purposes.

Predict that the popular technique of augmenting zero-shot classifiers with LLM-generated class descriptions ("a tiger has stripes...") provides no gain over properly tuned generic prompt templates, its reported improvements being baseline-tuning artifacts.

Test whether the long-standing negative result that adversarial training fails to generalize across perturbation types (L∞→L2, pixel→spatial) persists at foundation-model scale, against the increasingly voiced hope that scale induces general robustness.

Predict that multi-view (>2) contrastive formulations provide no representation-quality benefit over standard two-view training at matched compute, with multi-crop's celebrated gains attributable entirely to its resolution asymmetry, not view count.

Test the null that the feature-alignment domain-adaptation literature (adversarial alignment, discrepancy minimization) provides no gain over the trivial pipeline of target-statistics normalization update plus confidence-filtered pseudo-labeling, at modern backbone strength.

Predict that regularization- and architecture-based continual-learning methods developed on small benchmarks provide no benefit over naive experience replay when applied to foundation-model fine-tuning sequences, where replay is cheap and forgetting dynamics differ.

Test the null that visual prompt tuning (learnable input/latent tokens) offers no advantage over a parameter-matched linear or shallow head for adapting frozen backbones on dense and classification tasks.

Predict that the consistency-regularization semi-supervised learning stack (FixMatch-style) adds nothing over simple fine-tuning of modern pretrained backbones on the labeled subset alone, across realistic label budgets.

Test the null that SAM-family optimizers, celebrated on ImageNet-1k-scale training, provide no generalization benefit at large data scale — their gains being a small-data regularization effect that vanishes when data supplies the regularization.

Test whether attention-head importance rankings — the basis of head-pruning methods and mechanistic claims about specialized heads — replicate across random seeds of the same training run, predicting they largely do not.

Run a preregistered falsification tournament testing whether any popular post-hoc calibration method (temperature scaling, vector scaling, spline, histogram binning) maintains calibration under even mild distribution shift, predicting all fail and shift-stable calibration requires different machinery.

Characterize the failure conditions of "segmentation emerges from caption supervision alone" claims, predicting the emergent grouping collapses on cluttered multi-object scenes and stuff regions — the majority of real pixels — and exists mainly for centered single objects.

Test the null that retrieval-augmented visual classification (retrieving similar labeled images at test time) provides no benefit once near-duplicate and same-source leakage between retrieval database and test sets is removed.

Predict that dataset distillation — compressing datasets into small synthetic sets — produces sets so architecture-specific that training any architecture other than the distillation target on them fails, nullifying the "compressed dataset" interpretation.

Test the null that mixup's celebrated calibration improvement is entirely reproducible by temperature scaling a mixup-free model — i.e., mixup changes confidence scale, not the confidence-accuracy relationship's informativeness.

Predict that defenses removing "frequency shortcuts" (spectral filtering, frequency augmentation) improve scores on synthetic corruption benchmarks while providing zero gain on natural distribution shifts — the defenses overfit the benchmark's frequency structure rather than fixing shortcut learning.

Re-test the capacity-gap phenomenon (distillation quality non-monotone in teacher size) with modern VLM/foundation teachers, predicting it persists — the biggest available teacher remains the wrong choice — against the practitioner default of always distilling from the largest model.

Test the null that chain-of-thought prompting improves multimodal *perception* accuracy (recognition, counting, OCR, localization), as opposed to multi-step reasoning tasks — predicting zero or negative effects because verbalization cannot add visual information and may overwrite it with priors.

Run controlled user studies testing the null that providing state-of-the-art attribution maps does not improve ML practitioners' actual model-debugging performance (finding planted bugs: spurious cues, label errors, backdoors) over seeing only inputs, predictions, and confidences.

Test the null that slot-based object-centric representation learning, at matched pretraining compute, provides no advantage over plain patch-based features for the downstream reasoning and prediction tasks it was designed to enable.

Test the null that inserting an intermediate fine-tuning task between pretraining and target fine-tuning ("stepping-stone transfer") provides no reliable benefit for vision tasks, with published positive cases being selection effects over a distribution centered at zero.

Test whether the historical correlation between ImageNet accuracy and downstream transfer quality — the field's core model-selection heuristic — has broken down for post-2021 high-accuracy models, predicting near-zero rank correlation within the modern frontier cohort.

Test the null that the universal practice of filtering pseudo-labels by confidence threshold selects no better than randomly keeping the same volume of pseudo-labels, because confidence correlates with easiness in ways that make retained labels redundant rather than informative.

Show that mIoU is so dominated by large-region interiors that method rankings on popular segmentation benchmarks change substantially under size-stratified and boundary-weighted decompositions — meaning the field's headline metric cannot see much of what methods differ in.

Audit the silent variation in test-time preprocessing (resize kernels, crop protocols, normalization constants, padding) across segmentation/detection codebases, quantifying how much of cross-paper "improvement" is reproducible preprocessing artifact.

Decompose the last decade of COCO detection AP improvements into localization-quality gains versus classification/recognition gains, testing the hypothesis that recent progress is almost entirely localization refinement — a much narrower achievement than "better object understanding."

Quantify how much open-vocabulary segmentation/detection evaluation, which requires predicting the benchmark's exact class-name token, penalizes semantically correct predictions (synonyms, hypernyms), and show that semantic-similarity-aware scoring changes method rankings.

Show that the standard center-crop/resize evaluation protocol hides systematic failures on natural aspect ratios and compositions, and that model rankings shift when evaluation preserves native geometry — the protocol having quietly shaped models toward crop-world statistics.

Document how nominally identical benchmarks (ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO variants) exist in silently divergent versions across codebases — different label mappings, ignored-class conventions, split files, and annotation revisions — and quantify the cross-paper comparability error this creates.

Show that boundary-tolerant evaluation conventions (void bands around ground-truth boundaries, tolerance radii) are gameable: models can gain benchmark points by strategically hedging predictions in tolerance zones without any real boundary improvement.

Demonstrate that segmentation models with indistinguishable mIoU differ drastically in pixelwise confidence reliability (calibration, selective-prediction value), and propose reliability-adjusted dense evaluation that reorders methods for safety-relevant use.

Quantify the fraction of claimed state-of-the-art margins in segmentation/detection attributable to inference-time protocol choices (multi-scale testing, flipping, sliding-window overlap, threshold tuning) rather than to the proposed methods, via a protocol-normalized re-evaluation of recent leaderboard entries.

Measure the "paraphrase penalty" that exact-match and consensus-based VQA metrics impose on modern generative VLMs (correct answers phrased differently), and show metric choice — not capability — explains a meaningful share of cross-model ranking on legacy VQA benchmarks.

Quantify verbosity, confidence-phrasing, and style biases of LLM/VLM judges used in multimodal evaluation, and measure how much of current leaderboard ordering is explained by bias-susceptible presentation rather than content correctness.

Measure the contamination rate of popular multimodal benchmarks (test images or near-duplicates present in public pretraining corpora), and produce decontaminated re-rankings testing whether contamination advantages differ across models.

Perform a power analysis of few-shot evaluation protocols showing that the episode counts standard in the literature yield confidence intervals wider than typical claimed method differences — making a substantial fraction of few-shot leaderboard ordering statistical noise.

Show that the severity calibration of standard corruption-robustness benchmarks is inconsistent across corruption types (severity 3 fog ≠ severity 3 noise in any perceptual or informational sense), so aggregate robustness scores hide arbitrary weightings and re-normalization changes model rankings.

Audit the open secret that "zero-shot" cross-dataset segmentation/detection evaluations use hyperparameters (score thresholds, mask-fusion settings, prompt templates) tuned on the target benchmark, quantifying how much reported zero-shot performance depends on this hidden supervision.

Quantify how flat-label evaluation penalizes predictions that are correct at a finer granularity than the benchmark ontology ("oak" scored wrong against "tree"), and show hierarchy-aware scoring changes both rankings and the apparent scaling behavior of open-vocabulary models.

Analyze how the specific arithmetic of the Panoptic Quality metric (hard 0.5-IoU matching, equal thing/stuff averaging, small-segment sensitivity) has steered panoptic architecture evolution, and show that defensible alternative formulations reorder methods and would have favored different designs.

Run controlled human studies comparing perceived segmentation quality against metric rankings, testing whether mIoU-preferred outputs are actually preferred by application-representative human judges — and derive a perceptual segmentation metric from the disagreement structure.

Test the stability of multi-dataset meta-benchmark conclusions (VTAB-style suites, multimodal leaderboard aggregates) under defensible reweightings of constituent datasets, hypothesizing that many headline model orderings invert within the space of reasonable weights.

Construct fresh, protocol-matched replication test sets for detection/segmentation benchmarks and measure the "adaptive overfitting" gap — how much published method rankings and margins shrink on data nobody could have tuned against.

Quantify the fraction of referring-expression and grounding benchmarks solvable without the image — from expression statistics and dataset priors alone — and publish prior-resistant splits that force genuine visual grounding.

Quantify the inflation introduced by reporting the best checkpoint/epoch selected using test (or reused-validation) performance — a widespread quiet practice — and measure its aggregate effect on the field's reported margins.

Show that per-class IoU estimates for rare classes in standard benchmarks rest on so few test regions that their confidence intervals span several points of mIoU, and a substantial fraction of claimed improvements is attributable to statistically insignificant rare-class fluctuations.

Demonstrate that saturated threshold-based depth-estimation metrics (δ<1.25 family) no longer discriminate among modern monocular depth models whose errors are structural (planes, boundaries, scale drift), and that structure-sensitive evaluation reorders current methods.

Test whether the simulated-click protocols used to evaluate interactive segmentation (center-of-error-region clicking) produce method rankings that disagree with rankings under real human clicking behavior, invalidating the simulation as a selection instrument.

Audit vision-language compositionality benchmarks (binding, word-order tests) for statistical artifacts (caption plausibility asymmetries, image-quality cues) that allow high scores without compositional understanding, and construct artifact-controlled versions measuring how much reported "compositionality" survives.

Measure the effective distributional distance between training corpora and the benchmarks used to claim OOD robustness, testing whether celebrated "OOD generalization" results actually operate at small effective shifts for web-pretrained models — and recalibrate robustness claims per unit of measured shift.

Decompose video-object-segmentation evaluation to show that the standard first-frame-mask protocol mixes two abilities — appearance re-identification and mask propagation quality — such that methods ranked identically overall differ drastically per ability, and applications need the decomposed report.

Analyze how mask-AP's handling of ranked predictions rewards strategic duplicate and near-duplicate guessing (confidence-ordered variants of the same object), quantify how much current methods exploit this, and propose duplicate-penalized AP that changes rankings.

Estimate the aggregate false-discovery rate of one year of segmentation/detection SOTA claims by systematically re-running a random sample of published improvements with proper seed statistics, matched tuning, and held-out evaluation — turning meta-scientific criticism into a measured quantity.

Show that the same backbone can be corruption-robust for classification while fragile for segmentation (and vice versa), refuting the implicit assumption that robustness rankings transfer across tasks built on one representation.

Test whether the celebrated finding that spurious correlations live in the last layer (fixable by last-layer retraining) breaks down for dense prediction, where spurious cues (context textures, co-occurring backgrounds) are spatially entangled with features throughout the network.

Decompose adverse-weather failures of driving-scene segmentation into physical components (occlusion by drops, wet-surface reflections, contrast loss, color shift), testing the hypothesis that reflective-surface confusion — not the visually salient rain streaks — causes most safety-relevant errors.

Characterize the spatial propagation law of localized adversarial patches in dense prediction — how far beyond the patch predictions get corrupted — and show the propagation radius is architecture-family-dependent (global attention spreads corruption much farther than convolution).

Audit "natural adversarial example" benchmarks (ImageNet-A-style) to quantify what fraction of items reflect genuine model failure versus label ambiguity, multi-object scenes, and misleading ground truth — testing whether the benchmark measures robustness or annotation philosophy.

Measure how robustness interventions (augmentation families, adversarial training, ensembling, test-time adaptation) compose when stacked, testing the hypothesis of strongly sub-additive returns — the interventions consume a shared robustness resource rather than adding independent protections.

Characterize the failure boundary of test-time adaptation (TTA) methods under realistic non-i.i.d. test streams — temporally correlated inputs, label shift, recurring environments — hypothesizing catastrophic self-reinforcing drift precisely in the deployment conditions TTA is marketed for.

Perform an honest accounting of certified-robustness guarantees for dense prediction, testing whether achievable certified radii at deployable accuracy are orders of magnitude below physically meaningful threat sizes — and identify exactly where the certification pipeline loses tightness.

Establish a quantitative trade-off law between randomized-smoothing-based certification strength and boundary localization precision in segmentation — smoothing certifies interiors by destroying exactly the high-frequency evidence boundaries need.

Quantify the sensitivity of recognition/segmentation models to camera image-signal-processor (ISP) parameters — demosaicing, tone mapping, sharpening, denoising — by re-rendering RAW captures under controlled ISP variation, testing whether ISP shift causes degradation comparable to or exceeding celebrated environmental shifts.

Test the counterintuitive hypothesis that video-trained models are *more* fragile to motion blur than image-trained models — because temporal redundancy lets video models avoid learning blur-invariant single-frame features — inverting the natural expectation that video training teaches motion robustness.

Show that distribution shift induces systematic *directional* prediction bias (toward frequent, contextually expected classes) rather than symmetric accuracy loss, meaning rare and safety-critical classes vanish from predictions first — a failure structure aggregate robustness metrics cannot see.

Test at scale whether robustness gained from corruption-style augmentation generalizes to genuinely held-out corruption families, or whether the field's augmentation recipes amount to memorizing the benchmark's corruption manifold.

Demonstrate that multi-sensor fusion models (RGB+depth, RGB+LiDAR), advertised as robustness solutions, perform *worse* than their best single-modality branch when one sensor degrades — because learned fusion weights are static while sensor reliability is dynamic — and characterize when fusion is a liability.

Establish a quantitative law relating object pixel size to corruption robustness — how detection/segmentation reliability decays with size under each shift type — providing the missing input for safety analyses that currently assume size-uniform degradation.

Test the hypothesis that web-trained modern models are *more* sensitive to JPEG/codec parameter shifts than ImageNet-era models — because web training data is pre-compressed within a narrow quality band, creating an unrecognized codec-distribution dependence.
