Resolve the conflicting evidence on whether adversarially trained backbones transfer better or worse by testing a crossover hypothesis: robust features win dense-task transfer at low target-data scale (better priors) but lose at high scale (information ceiling from invariance constraints).

Establish frame-to-frame prediction instability (flicker) of segmentation models on videos as a robustness dimension uncorrelated with mIoU, propose its standardized measurement, and show that accuracy-matched models differ by large factors in stability — with training-procedure causes identifiable.

Characterize the *topology* of failure under distribution shift — CNN errors clustering in local image regions while ViT errors manifest as global, image-wide label coherence failures — showing architecture choice determines failure geometry, not just failure rate, with distinct safety implications.

Measure robustness under *combinations* of individually mild corruptions (slight blur + slight noise + slight color shift), testing the hypothesis that degradation composes super-linearly — real-world conditions are compositions, and single-axis benchmarks systematically understate deployed risk.

Characterize the backdoor threat surface of segmentation models, testing the hypothesis that dense tasks are substantially easier to backdoor imperceptibly than classification — spatially localized triggers causing spatially localized mislabeling evade all current defenses designed for image-level flips.

Audit the stability of promptable segmentation models (SAM-class) under tiny prompt perturbations — single-pixel point jitter, box edge shifts — documenting discontinuous mask changes and establishing prompt-stability as a reliability metric that current leaderboards ignore.

Show that models with equal mean robustness differ enormously in per-image worst-case behavior across shifts (some images fail under *every* condition), and that mean-based robustness reporting systematically hides the tail structure that determines real-world reliability.

Show that stylization-based robustness evaluations (and trainings) preserve scene layout statistics, so they measure only appearance-shift robustness while real domain shifts change layout too — inflating robustness estimates for models that rely on spatial priors.

Demonstrate that segmentation models under shift can maintain respectable mIoU while entire object instances vanish from predictions — pixel- and instance-level robustness decouple — and introduce instance-survival metrics that expose safety-relevant failures aggregate metrics miss.

Quantify how dense-prediction performance varies across world regions and income levels, and — beyond documenting the gap — attribute it causally among object-appearance differences, context/layout differences, and photographic-capture differences to determine what data collection would actually fix it.

Test the core assumption of simulation-based robustness testing — that failure modes discovered in simulation predict real-world failures — by systematically searching for failures in sim and verifying their transfer rate on matched real captures.

Re-attribute the robustness advantages claimed for architectural innovations by retraining architecture pairs on strictly matched data and recipes, testing the hypothesis that data differences explain most published cross-architecture robustness differences.

Test the hypothesis that large pretrained models are more robust than small models to random (symmetric) label noise during fine-tuning but *less* robust to structured, instance-dependent noise — because their capacity and priors let them internalize systematic error patterns that small models cannot fit.

Show that selective-prediction (abstention) mechanisms tuned in-distribution invert under shift — the model abstains on hard-but-solvable ID-like items while confidently answering the shifted items it gets wrong — and establish shift-robust abstention evaluation as a required reporting standard.

Test whether a single cheap quantity — functional distance from the pretrained initialization (output KL on unlabeled data) — predicts the generalization gap of fine-tuned models better than the classical complexity-measure zoo.

Test whether the celebrated linear ID-OOD accuracy relationship — which underpins how the field interprets robustness interventions — holds for segmentation and detection, where spatial error structure and per-class coupling could break the law.

Empirically test the theory that memorizing rare training examples is *necessary* for tail generalization, by estimating per-example memorization scores at modern scale and measuring the causal effect of removing memorized examples on tail-class test accuracy.

Test the parsimony hypothesis that texture bias, shortcut learning, and adversarial vulnerability — treated as three literatures — are manifestations of one measurable quantity (the model's effective spectral/simplicity bias), such that a single intervention moves all three predictably.

Replicate and extend the negative result that flatness/sharpness measures fail to predict generalization once architecture varies, at foundation-model scale — testing whether the field's favorite generalization story survives its most basic out-of-family test.

Test whether generalization to novel classes (open-set recognition) and generalization to novel domains (distribution shift) — habitually conflated as "generalization ability" — are actually uncorrelated model properties with different data and architectural determinants.

Test whether models whose error patterns match human confusion structure (before any shift) generalize better under distribution shift — making human-alignment of errors a cheap, ID-computable robustness predictor.

Establish that models compose visual concepts (attribute-object, object-context) exactly as far as the compositional statistics of training data allow — a measurable "visual n-gram" law — reframing compositional failure from an architecture problem to a data-statistics bound.

Test a conservation-like trade-off in VLMs: models that store more task knowledge in weights (better zero-shot) are systematically worse at in-context adaptation to conflicting or novel information, and vice versa — the two learning modes competing rather than composing.

Attribute each of a trained model's invariances (translation, scale, rotation tolerance, illumination) quantitatively to architecture (built-in constraints) versus data statistics (learned exposure), producing an invariance provenance map that tests the belief that data can teach any invariance.

Causally test the celebrated distribution-robustness of CLIP-style models by retraining on corpora with style-shifted content (sketches, renditions, art) explicitly removed, predicting that the famous effective-robustness collapses to standard levels — closing the debate with an intervention rather than correlation.

Test whether per-sample difficulty is model-independent enough that a single score — k-NN distance in a fixed pretrained feature space — predicts the errors of arbitrary downstream models (architectures, tasks, training data) at practically useful accuracy.

Test whether the widely studied neural-collapse geometry (simplex ETF structure of last-layer features) has any causal relevance to generalization by training models with collapse explicitly prevented and showing unchanged downstream behavior.

Show that a measurable diversity statistic of the pretraining corpus — not its raw size — predicts downstream few-shot sample efficiency, by constructing same-size corpora of controlled diversity and measuring adaptation curves.

Test whether VLMs apply relational knowledge acquired purely through text (size relations, part structures, physical properties never depicted in training images) to visual tasks — a direct measurement of cross-modal knowledge transfer that the multimodal paradigm presumes but rarely verifies.

Audit learned pipeline components (learned optimizers, learned augmentation policies, learned loss functions) for catastrophic meta-overfitting — strong performance within their meta-training task distribution and silent failure outside it — with a transferable measurement protocol for "meta-generalization radius."

Show that dataset pruning at high ratios does not merely approximate full-data training but *changes the generalization profile* — pruned-trained models losing ID accuracy while gaining OOD robustness — because pruning metrics preferentially remove distribution-core redundancy and retain boundary/rare structure.

Measure the "underspecification volume" of modern training pipelines — how differently identically-scoring models can behave OOD — across model scale, testing the uncomfortable hypothesis that scale *increases* the behavioral spread of equivalent models rather than pinning it down.

Quantify how much of measured cross-dataset performance drops in segmentation/detection stems from annotation-convention differences (boundary placement, class definitions, granularity, void handling) rather than image-distribution shift — by re-annotating image subsets under both conventions.

Test whether model scaling improves generalization to genuinely novel geometric conditions (unseen viewpoints, extreme scales, unusual object orientations) or only densifies interpolation within seen conditions — predicting flat or negative scaling curves for true geometric extrapolation.

Map when task-vector arithmetic (adding/subtracting fine-tuning weight deltas) works, testing the hypothesis that semantic task edits compose linearly while spatially structured task edits (dense tasks, localization) interfere destructively — a predictable boundary defined by task type.

Decompose out-of-distribution performance drops into feature-space failure (information lost) versus readout misalignment (information present, classifier miscalibrated to shifted geometry), by measuring how much of each gap a small-sample readout refit recovers across many shift types.

Characterize the *shape* (not just level) of accuracy-vs-shift-magnitude curves across model scales, testing the hypothesis that small models degrade convexly (graceful) while large models degrade concavely (cliff-like) — better average robustness purchased with sharper failure onset.

Test whether the operative variable in pretraining-data quality is per-image scene complexity (object count, occlusion, layout richness) rather than the corpus-level category diversity the field optimizes, by constructing corpora that decouple the two.

Test the counterintuitive allocation hypothesis that adding more *head-class* data improves tail-class performance — because tail classes are recognized through compositional reuse of features refined on head classes — inverting the standard rebalancing prescription.

Show that removing a shortcut cue from training does not produce robust features but shifts reliance to the next-simplest available cue — a measurable, ordered cue hierarchy — implying shortcut mitigation must address the hierarchy, not individual cues.

Test the hypothesis that data deduplication — an unquestioned hygiene step — *harms* training in small-data regimes, where natural duplication acts as beneficial importance weighting, making dedup policy scale-dependent rather than universal.

Show that selecting checkpoints/hyperparameters by ID validation accuracy systematically picks less shift-robust models than selecting by cheap unlabeled invariance statistics (prediction consistency under augmentation on unlabeled target-like data) — challenging the universal selection practice.

Test the hypothesis that most of the synthetic-to-real transfer gap for segmentation is carried by low-level image statistics (color distribution, noise, frequency spectra) fixable with cheap statistical alignment — and that the celebrated "content/semantic gap" is a minor residual.

Establish that fine-grained downstream capability is bounded by a computable pretraining resolution/patch-size ceiling — features for details smaller than the effective sampling scale cannot exist and are not recoverable by fine-tuning — replacing "more data/capacity will fix it" expectations with a hard law.

Build and validate an autonomous agent pipeline that re-executes published vision experiments from paper+code artifacts, producing the first literature-scale replication census and a taxonomy of why vision results fail to reproduce.

Measure the calibration of computer-vision researchers' beliefs by eliciting forecasts on which published improvements will replicate (before running the replications), testing whether the community's intuition carries any signal — and publishing the calibration curve.

Measure the decay of published training tricks' effectiveness as base recipes evolve — fitting "half-life curves" for a sample of once-beneficial techniques re-evaluated under successive recipe generations — to quantify how much of the methods literature is transient recipe-interaction.

Quantify the divergence between academic impact (citations) and real adoption (presence in production configs, framework defaults, competition-winning solutions) for vision methods, characterizing what the two selection processes each reward.

Systematically re-test the classical segmentation toolbox (CRFs, superpixels, contour grouping, MRF priors) on top of modern foundation features, testing the hypothesis that several "obsolete" structured methods become competitive again once their unary terms are strong — a directed archaeology of discarded ideas.

Run a controlled multi-team experiment where independent groups implement the same method from its paper description alone, measuring the distribution of results attributable purely to implementation degrees of freedom — the field's unquantified "implementation noise floor."

Fit lifecycle models to the historical trajectories of vision benchmarks (adoption, discrimination power, saturation, post-saturation misuse) and test whether the fitted dynamics predict — in advance — when current benchmarks will stop discriminating between methods.

Estimate the volume and content of unpublished negative results in vision research through structured researcher surveys and lab-notebook sampling, quantifying the file-drawer effect's size and identifying which "known-not-to-work" knowledge the community keeps re-purchasing.

Re-plot the last decade of segmentation/detection progress normalized by training compute and data cost, testing whether efficiency-adjusted progress has stalled — separating genuine algorithmic advance from resource escalation.

Measure the contamination of published vision papers with LLM-artifact errors — hallucinated references, misattributed claims, subtly wrong technical statements matching known LLM failure patterns — and model the propagation dynamics of such errors through subsequent citation.

Quantify the run-to-run performance variation attributable purely to hardware/software nondeterminism (kernel scheduling, cuDNN algorithm selection, driver versions) at fixed seeds, comparing this irreducible noise floor against the margins claimed in recent dense-prediction papers.

Pilot adversarial collaboration — proponents and skeptics of a contested vision claim jointly preregister decisive experiments — on two live controversies (e.g., "language supervision improves dense features" and "attention is necessary at scale"), evaluating the protocol itself as a dispute-resolution instrument for the field.
